question_text: A hospital wants a model that identifies its most effective nurses. The data team proposes using each nurse's average patient-satisfaction survey score as the target label. What should the team do first?
hint: Ask whether the label measures the concept management actually cares about.
correct_answer_citation: Every people-analytics project must therefore audit the target variable for measurement bias before evaluating predictive accuracy.

options.option_text: Train several models and keep the one with the highest accuracy on the survey scores
options.option_explanation: High accuracy on a flawed label only means the model reproduces the flaw more faithfully.

options.option_text: Check how well survey scores capture nursing effectiveness, and whether they are biased
options.option_explanation: Correct. Survey scores may miss safety work and mentoring and may reflect patient bias, so the label must be audited before accuracy means anything.

options.option_text: Add more features, such as shift length and ward, to raise predictive power
options.option_explanation: More features do not fix a target label that measures the wrong thing.

options.option_text: Replace the survey score with years of tenure, since tenure is objective
options.option_explanation: Tenure is another proxy with its own gaps. Being easy to count does not make it a valid measure of effectiveness.

prompt: A logistics company is hiring a supply chain planner. Sort each screening behavior by the kind of system that produces it.

cards.text: Rejects a resume that says "inventory optimization" because it never uses the phrase "supply chain"
cards.explanation: Different terminology for the same skill fails an exact-match rule.

cards.text: Ranks a procurement analyst highly because purchasing forecasts sit next to demand planning in the skills graph
cards.explanation: A skills taxonomy connects adjacent skills, so related experience counts.

cards.text: Passes a resume that repeats "supply chain" ten times in white text at the bottom
cards.explanation: Counting words rewards stuffing rather than demonstrated capability.

cards.text: Reads a two-column PDF and a plain-text resume into the same fields for past roles and outcomes
cards.explanation: Language models extract varied resume formats into a common schema.

cards.text: Flags an overlooked candidate from the military logistics corps for a recruiter to read
cards.explanation: Well-designed semantic screening surfaces candidates for human review.

cards.text: Drops an applicant who wrote "SCM" instead of the posting's full wording
cards.explanation: An abbreviation is a terminology mismatch that exact matching cannot see past.

prompt: An internal talent marketplace suggests a next role for each employee. Match each employee to the role they are most closely adjacent to.

pairs.term: Payroll clerk who reconciles accounts and builds spreadsheet formulas
pairs.explanation: Reconciliation and spreadsheet modeling transfer directly to entry-level financial analysis.

pairs.term: Retail store trainer who writes onboarding guides and runs workshops
pairs.explanation: Designing and delivering training is the core of the target role.

pairs.term: Warehouse dispatcher who schedules trucks and tracks delivery delays
pairs.explanation: Scheduling and delay tracking are the main tasks of logistics planning.

pairs.term: IT help desk technician who scripts password resets and reads system logs
pairs.explanation: Scripting and log reading leave a small training gap to systems administration.

prompt: A hospital is deploying AI across a nurse manager's role. Sort each task by whether software would take it over or help the person do it better.

cards.text: Turning the end-of-shift voice note into a typed log entry
cards.explanation: Transcription follows codifiable rules, so software can replace the human step.

cards.text: Deciding how to staff a ward during a flu surge, with a model suggesting options
cards.explanation: The model raises the quality of a complex judgment the manager still makes.

cards.text: Sorting supply invoices into budget categories
cards.explanation: Categorizing receipts is a routine subtask software can take over.

cards.text: Preparing for a difficult conversation with a patient's family, using an AI to rehearse
cards.explanation: Empathy and context stay with the person, and AI helps them prepare.

cards.text: Formatting the weekly rota into the standard hospital template
cards.explanation: Formatting routine reports is a classic automation example.

cards.text: Analyzing a medication-error incident, with AI drafting a timeline for review
cards.explanation: AI speeds up analysis while the manager judges causes and remedies.

question_text: A law firm gives every lawyer an AI drafting assistant. Which outcome best fits the pattern from field experiments?
hint: Think about who gains most, and what happens on tasks outside the model's competence.
correct_answer_citation: On tasks outside the model's competence, workers who uncritically accept AI outputs perform worse than workers who use no AI at all, making human domain judgment essential.

options.option_text: Senior partners gain the most, because they know how to write the best prompts
options.option_explanation: Field experiments find the opposite: the largest percentage gains go to less-experienced workers.

options.option_text: Every lawyer improves by roughly the same percentage on every kind of task
options.option_explanation: Gains are uneven across workers and can turn negative on tasks outside the frontier.

options.option_text: First-year associates speed up most, but those who copy AI output on a novel legal question do worse than with no AI
options.option_explanation: Correct. Novices gain most inside the frontier, while uncritical acceptance outside it makes performance worse than working without AI.

options.option_text: Output quality falls for most lawyers, because the assistant writes in a generic style
options.option_explanation: Inside the frontier, quality rises, especially for lower performers.

question_text: An online aptitude test passes 150 of 300 applicants aged under 40 and 60 of 200 applicants aged 40 and over. Does the four-fifths rule indicate adverse impact?
hint: Compute each group's selection rate, then compare the lower rate with 80 percent of the higher one.
correct_answer_citation: Adverse impact is indicated if the selection rate for any protected race, sex, or ethnic group is less than 80 percent (four-fifths) of the rate for the group with the highest selection rate.

options.option_text: No, because more applicants aged 40 and over were tested than the rule requires
options.option_explanation: The rule compares selection rates, not the number of applicants tested.

options.option_text: No, because 60 passes is at least four-fifths of the 75 passes expected
options.option_explanation: The comparison uses each group's selection rate against the highest group's rate, not expected counts.

options.option_text: Yes, because 30% is below the 40% threshold (0.80 × 50%)
options.option_explanation: Correct. Under 40: 150 / 300 = 50%. Aged 40 and over: 60 / 200 = 30%. The threshold is 0.80 × 50% = 40%, and 30% falls below it.

options.option_text: Yes, because fewer than half of all applicants passed the test
options.option_explanation: The overall pass rate does not matter. The rule compares groups with each other.

prompt: A software company reviews its workplace data practices. For each practice, name what it is.

cases.text: Tracking the median time code waits for review across all teams, with no names attached
cases.explanation: It is aggregated and anonymized, and it points to a process bottleneck.

cases.text: Capturing a screenshot of each developer's screen every ten minutes
cases.explanation: Continuous individual capture of activity is covert-style monitoring that erodes trust.

cases.text: After commit counts are tied to bonuses, developers split each change into many tiny commits
cases.explanation: The activity proxy became a target and stopped measuring real output.

cases.text: Running sentiment analysis on employees' private chat messages
cases.explanation: Private message scanning is named as invasive individual surveillance.

cases.text: Measuring average handoff delay between design and engineering each sprint
cases.explanation: Team-level workflow data used to remove a bottleneck sits inside the governance boundary.

cases.text: Once 'hours shown online' is ranked, staff leave their chat status active overnight
cases.explanation: Gaming a narrow activity measure once it becomes a target is Goodhart's Law.
